Twenty five monsters from around the world, and the real story behind every one.

Left page tells you where the monster comes from and what people actually said about it. Right page is that monster caught in the middle of doing the thing it is famous for, waiting for your crayons.

Ages 4 to 12. Nothing gory, nothing frightening.

A friendly horse is waiting by the water. Do not get on its back.

The kelpie is one of the oldest warnings in Scotland, and underneath the story is a piece of very practical advice about deep cold water and children who wander near it.

Every parent knows this exact scene.

This one is the strigoi, from Romania, who was never a stranger. It was somebody from your own village who had died and come back, wandering the lanes after dark and bothering the animals.

Your kid just wants to stay up.

His feet point backwards, so his tracks send you the wrong way.

The curupira guards the forest and the animals in it. Hunters who take more than they need are the ones who end up walking in circles until morning.

Bow to a kappa and it has to bow back. When it bows, the dish of water on its head spills, and a kappa without its water is a much less confident creature.

Politeness as a survival tactic is a very Japanese solution to a monster problem.

One flap of his fan and your hat is somewhere over the mountain.

The tengu started out as a straightforward menace and slowly became something more complicated. In later stories he is a teacher, and swordsmen climb the mountain hoping to be trained by him.

The goats have done the maths.

You hear her crying by the river a long time before you see her.

La Llorona is told across Mexico and much of Latin America, and almost everybody who grew up with her heard a slightly different version from a slightly different relative.

Something in the waterhole has just made an enormous noise.

The bunyip comes from Aboriginal Australian stories, and nobody agrees on what it looks like. Every account describes something different, which is part of why it is still frightening.

The jiangshi hops because its arms are stuck out straight in front of it.

The stories come from bodies being carried home over long distances so they could be buried in the right place. The hopping is the part everybody remembers.

Relatable on a Monday.

If you hear her crying outside, somebody in the family is about to die.

The banshee does not cause anything. She announces it. In the older Irish stories she is attached to particular families and has been following them for generations.

The strigoi was never a stranger. It was somebody from your own village who had died and then come back, wandering the lanes after dark and bothering the animals.

The word vampire only reached English in the 1730s, from news reports out of Eastern Europe. Bram Stoker wrote his famous book much later, in 1897. The cape and the evening suit came later still, from a stage play and then a film.

In Iceland the Yule Cat is watching what you are wearing.

Anybody who did not get a new piece of clothing before Christmas was said to be fair game. Underneath it is a story about wool, and about finishing the autumn work before the nights closed in.

So yes, socks count.

Her house has chicken legs, and it walks around the forest at night.
